doc.title: Ira Gitler interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995

title: Can jazz be America's popular music again
summary: Gitler doubts it; big bands are uneconomical, though Jimmy Heath's band at the Iridium shows interest, and he recalls 1940s Sunday jam sessions.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Can — and this is kind of a follow-up — can jazz, you know for instance we talk about the big band period and we say how two great things, people were dancing and people were listening on the radio. Can jazz ever become America’s popular music again?

Looking at it right now, I don’t think so, but who knows? That was a particular time, if you’re talking about big bands, you know economically it’s not feasible. In fact if you have a sextet and you want to book it, you’re probably better off cutting it back to a quintet because you might have a better chance, right? And big bands exist now in little places once a week or some bands have existed getting bookings, you know going to Europe and Japan and all that, but the big band is not a viable thing. Once ballrooms ceased and theater stage shows and hotel rooms where bands played, you know the venues dried up. And if you are a club owner, you put a big band in and you have a bigger nut to cover. I heard Jimmy Heath’s big band recently, which is not together all the time by any means, and they played over at the Iridium, one of New York’s newer clubs, it’s only been a couple of years. And I’m sure that everybody was making scale, they weren’t making a lot of money, but it took a lot of courage to put a big band in there for a week, and people dug it, and I think they’re going to go back in. There’s nothing quite like a big band in full roar, and you can’t duplicate that. But I don’t think it’s going to come back in the same way. There’s no reason why people can’t dance to smaller combos. We used to have that. The people danced and the people that didn’t want to dance got up around the bandstand and listened, even at jam sessions, which I used to go to a lot in the forties. They had chairs set up in the back, these were organized jam sessions, a Sunday afternoon gig, that was the typical, traditional time for that, Sunday afternoon, late afternoon into early evening. And they’d set up chairs towards the back of the ballroom and leave space in the front for people to dance. So it was just the opposite of when you went to hear a big band and people danced in the back and people crowded up around the bandstand to listen. They pre-figured this.
